results.title: The standard 23-cycle in $M_{23}$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The permutation of $\{0, 1, \dots, 22\}$ that sends $i$ to $i + 1$ for $i < 22$ and sends $22$ to $0$, that is, the 23-cycle $(0\ 1\ 2\ \cdots\ 22)$. It is the first of the two standard generators of the Mathieu group $M_{23}$.

results.title: The standard product of four 5-cycles in $M_{23}$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The permutation of the points $\{0, 1, \dots, 22\}$ given by the product of the four disjoint 5-cycles $(2\ 16\ 9\ 6\ 8)(3\ 12\ 13\ 18\ 4)(7\ 17\ 10\ 11\ 22)(14\ 19\ 21\ 20\ 15)$, where a cycle $(a_1\ a_2\ \cdots\ a_5)$ sends $a_k$ to $a_{k+1}$ for $k < 5$ and sends $a_5$ to $a_1$. It fixes the three remaining points $0$, $1$ and $5$, and it is the second of the two standard generators of the Mathieu group $M_{23}$.

results.title: The Mathieu group $M_{23}$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The subgroup of the symmetric group on $\{0, 1, \dots, 22\}$ generated by the standard 23-cycle $(0\ 1\ 2\ \cdots\ 22)$ and the standard product of four disjoint 5-cycles $(2\ 16\ 9\ 6\ 8)(3\ 12\ 13\ 18\ 4)(7\ 17\ 10\ 11\ 22)(14\ 19\ 21\ 20\ 15)$.

results.title: Subgroups containing $M_{23}$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A subgroup $H$ of the symmetric group on $\{0, 1, \dots, 22\}$ contains the Mathieu group $M_{23}$ if and only if $H$ contains both the standard 23-cycle and the standard product of four 5-cycles that generate $M_{23}$.

results.title: Inversion on a group ring
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $G$ a commutative group. The inversion of the group ring $R[G]$ is the ring automorphism of $R[G]$ induced by the group automorphism $g \mapsto g^{-1}$ of $G$: it sends $\sum_g r_g\, g$ to $\sum_g r_g\, g^{-1}$.

results.title: Inversion on basis elements
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $G$ a commutative group. For every $g \in G$ and $r \in R$, the inversion of the group ring $R[G]$ sends $r\, g$ to $r\, g^{-1}$.

results.title: Group-ring inversion is an involution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a commutative group and $\iota$ the inversion of the group ring $R[G]$. For every $x \in R[G]$, $\iota(\iota(x)) = x$.

results.title: Inversion twist of a group-ring module
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a commutative group and $A$ a module over the group ring $R[G]$. The inversion twist of $A$ is a copy of $A$ with the same addition, on which $r \in R[G]$ acts by $a \mapsto \iota(r) \cdot a$, where $\iota$ is the inversion of $R[G]$ and $\cdot$ is the original action on $A$.

results.title: Underlying bijection of the inversion twist
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For every type $A$, the map sending an element of the inversion twist of $A$ to its underlying element of $A$ is a bijection, whose inverse sends $a \in A$ to its copy in the twist.

results.title: Scalar action on the inversion twist
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a commutative group and $A$ a module over the group ring $R[G]$. For every $r \in R[G]$ and every element $a$ of the inversion twist of $A$, with underlying element $\bar a \in A$, the underlying element of $r \cdot a$ is $\iota(r) \cdot \bar a$, where $\iota$ is the inversion of $R[G]$ and $\cdot$ on the right is the original action on $A$.

results.title: Twisting twice by inversion recovers the module
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a commutative group and $A$ a module over the group ring $R[G]$. The map sending an element of the inversion twist of the inversion twist of $A$ to its underlying element of $A$ is an $R[G]$-linear isomorphism.

results.title: Pure subgroups of abelian groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A subgroup $B$ of an abelian group $A$ is pure when $nA \cap B = nB$ for every integer $n$: for every integer $n$ and every $a \in A$ with $na \in B$ there is some $b \in B$ with $nb = na$.

results.title: MacHale's question on fully invariant subgroups (Kourovka 16.61)

results.title: Fully invariant subgroups of every order do not force cyclicity

results.summary: Not every finite group $G$ having, for every divisor $d$ of $|G|$, a fully invariant subgroup of order $d$ (a subgroup $H$ with $\varphi(H) \le H$ for every endomorphism $\varphi$ of $G$) is cyclic.

results.title: Jung's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $s$ be a bounded subset of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with diameter $\operatorname{diam} s$. Then there is a point $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $s$ is contained in the closed ball with center $c$ and radius $\sqrt{n / (2(n + 1))} \cdot \operatorname{diam} s$.

results.title: Kirchberger's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets of points in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Then $A$ and $B$ are strictly separated by a hyperplane, that is, there are a nonzero vector $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $\beta$ with $\langle w, a \rangle < \beta$ for all $a \in A$ and $\beta < \langle w, c \rangle$ for all $c \in B$, if and only if for every set $C \subseteq A \cup B$ of at most $d + 2$ points, the sets $A \cap C$ and…

results.title: Rado's centerpoint theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\mathbb{R}^d$, not necessarily distinct. Then some point $x$ in the convex hull of $\{p_1, \dots, p_n\}$ has at least $n/(d+1)$ of the points in every closed halfspace containing it: for all $v \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$ with $\langle v, x \rangle \le t$, the number of indices $i$ with $\langle v, p_i \rangle \le t$ is at least $n/(d+1)$.

results.title: Tverberg's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d, r$ be natural numbers with $r \ge 1$ and let $N = (d+1)(r-1)+1$. For any points $p_1, \dots, p_N$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, not necessarily distinct, there are pairwise disjoint sets $P_1, \dots, P_r \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ whose union is $\{1, \dots, N\}$ and a point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ that lies in the convex hull of $\{p_i : i \in P_j\}$ for every $j$.

results.title: Ulam's flat-sections problem in dimension three
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ be a compact set homeomorphic to the closed unit ball. Suppose that for every nonzero continuous linear functional $F : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ and every real $c$ such that the plane $\{x : F(x) = c\}$ meets the interior of $K$, the intersection of this plane with the boundary (frontier) of $K$ is homeomorphic to the unit circle. Then $K$ is convex.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be an additive commutative monoid, let $h, k \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a \colon \mathbb{N} \to G$ list the set $A = \{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{k-1}\}$; write $n x$ for the $n$-fold sum $x + \dots + x$. The trivial elements of the $h$-fold sumset $hA$ form the finite set that is empty when $k = 0$ and otherwise consists of $h a_0$ together with the sums $(h - i) a_j + i a_{j+1}$ for all natural numbers $i \le h$…

results.title: No trivial elements for $k = 0$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be an additive commutative monoid, $h$ a natural number and $a \colon \mathbb{N} \to G$. For $k = 0$, when $\{a_0, \dots, a_{k-1}\}$ is the empty set, the set of trivial elements of its $h$-fold sumset is empty.

results.title: Trivial elements of a one-element set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be an additive commutative monoid, $h$ a natural number and $a \colon \mathbb{N} \to G$. For $k = 1$, when $\{a_0, \dots, a_{k-1}\}$ is the one-element set $\{a_0\}$, the set of trivial elements of its $h$-fold sumset is exactly $\{h a_0\}$, where $h a_0 = a_0 + \dots + a_0$ is the $h$-fold sum of $a_0$.

results.title: Adjacent sums are trivial elements
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be an additive commutative monoid, $a_0, a_1, \ldots$ a sequence in $G$, and $h, k, i, j$ natural numbers with $j + 1 < k$ and $i \le h$. Then $(h - i)a_j + i a_{j+1}$ is a trivial element of the $h$-fold sumset of $a_0, \ldots, a_{k-1}$.

results.title: Characterization of the trivial elements
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be an additive commutative monoid, $a_0, a_1, \ldots$ a sequence in $G$, and $h, k$ natural numbers. An element $x \in G$ is a trivial element of the $h$-fold sumset of $a_0, \ldots, a_{k-1}$ if and only if either $k > 0$ and $x = h a_0$, or $x = (h - i)a_j + i a_{j+1}$ for some natural numbers $j$ and $i$ with $j + 1 < k$ and $i \le h$.

results.title: A gap in the possible sumset sizes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a torsion-free additive commutative group and let $h$ and $k \ge 4$ be natural numbers. For every $k$-element set $A \subseteq G$, the $h$-fold sumset $hA$ (the set of sums of $h$ elements of $A$) does not satisfy $hk - h + 2 \le |hA| \le hk - 1$.

results.title: Sumset sizes between $hk - h + 1$ and $hk$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a nontrivial torsion-free additive commutative group and let $h \ge 1$ and $k \ge 4$ be natural numbers. For a finite set $A \subseteq G$ write $hA$ for its $h$-fold sumset, the set of sums of $h$ elements of $A$, and write $R_G(h, k)$ for the set of sizes $|hA|$ of $k$-element sets $A \subseteq G$. Then $R_G(h, k) \cap [hk - h + 1, hk] = \{hk - h + 1, hk\}$.

results.title: Sumset of an arithmetic progression with its second-to-last term removed
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a linearly ordered additive commutative group, let $a \in G$ with $a > 0$, and let $k \ge 3$ and $h \ge 1$ be natural numbers. The set $A = \{0, a, 2a, \ldots, (k - 2)a, ka\}$, obtained from $\{0, a, 2a, \ldots, ka\}$ by removing $(k - 1)a$, has $|hA| = hk$, where $hA$ is the $h$-fold sumset of $A$, the set of sums of $h$ elements of $A$.

results.title: Rajagopal's family of missing sumset sizes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a torsion-free additive commutative group and let $h$, $k$ and $\ell$ be natural numbers with $\ell + 3 \le \min(h, k)$. For every $k$-element set $A \subseteq G$, the $h$-fold sumset $hA$ (the set of sums of $h$ elements of $A$) does not satisfy $hk - h + 2 + \ell h \le |hA| \le hk - h + 1 + \ell h + (h - 2 - \ell)$.

results.summary: For every $k \ge 4$ and every sufficiently large $n$ (depending on $k$), every family of more than $\binom{n-2}{k-2}$ subsets of $\{1, \dots, n\}$, each with exactly $k$ elements, contains two sets $A$ and $B$ with $|A \cap B| = 1$.

results.title: Frankl's theorem on families with no singleton intersection
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $k \ge 4$ and every sufficiently large $n$ (depending on $k$), every family of more than $\binom{n-2}{k-2}$ subsets of $\{1, \dots, n\}$, each with exactly $k$ elements, contains two sets $A$ and $B$ with $|A \cap B| = 1$.

results.title: Adjacency matrix
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, an adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices is a directed graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ given by a Boolean-valued function $\mathrm{adj}$ on ordered pairs of vertices: $\mathrm{adj}(i, j)$ is true exactly when there is a directed edge from $i$ to $j$.

results.title: Empty adjacency matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the empty adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices is the directed graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with no edges: its adjacency function is false on every ordered pair of vertices.

results.title: Edge query of an adjacency matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $i, j$, the edge query of $m$ at $(i, j)$ is the Boolean value that is true exactly when $m$ has a directed edge from $i$ to $j$.

results.title: The empty adjacency matrix has no edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$ and all vertices $i$ and $j$ among the $n$ vertices, the empty adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices has no edge from $i$ to $j$.

results.title: Edge insertion in an adjacency matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $i$ and $j$, adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ gives the adjacency matrix that has an edge from $i$ to $j$ and agrees with $m$ on every other ordered pair of vertices.

results.title: An inserted edge is present
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices $i$ and $j$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $i$ to $j$.

results.title: Inserting an edge leaves other pairs unchanged
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices $i$, $j$, $a$, $b$ with $a \ne i$ or $b \ne j$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $m$ does.

results.title: Edges after inserting an edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices $i$, $j$, $a$, $b$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $a = i$ and $b = j$, or $m$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$.

results.title: Edge deletion in an adjacency matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $i$ and $j$, removing the edge from $i$ to $j$ gives the adjacency matrix that has no edge from $i$ to $j$ and agrees with $m$ on every other ordered pair of vertices.

results.title: Deleting an edge removes it
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j$ be vertices. Then the graph obtained from $m$ by deleting the edge from $i$ to $j$ has no edge from $i$ to $j$.

results.title: Deleting an edge leaves the other entries unchanged

results.summary:

e i$ or $b 
e j$. Then the graph obtained from $m$ by deleting the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $m$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$.

results.title: Edges after deleting an edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices $i$, $j$, $a$, $b$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by removing the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $(a, b) \ne (i, j)$ and $m$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$.

results.title: Extensionality of adjacency matrices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Two adjacency matrices $m$ and $m'$ on the same $n$ vertices are equal if, for all vertices $i$ and $j$, $m$ has an edge from $i$ to $j$ exactly when $m'$ does.

results.title: Out-neighbor list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a vertex $i$, the out-neighbor list of $i$ is the list of all vertices $j$ such that $m$ has a directed edge from $i$ to $j$, in increasing order.

results.title: The out-neighbor list matches the edge query
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j$ be vertices. Then $j$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of $i$ if and only if $m$ has a directed edge from $i$ to $j$.

results.title: Out-neighbor lists have no duplicates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a vertex $i$, no vertex occurs twice in the out-neighbor list of $i$.

results.title: Out-neighbor lists are strictly increasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a vertex $i$, the out-neighbor list of $i$ is strictly increasing: every vertex in it is smaller than every vertex that comes after it.

results.title: Out-neighbor lists of the empty graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the graph with no edges on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the out-neighbor list of every vertex $i$ is the empty list.

results.title: Adding an edge makes its target an out-neighbor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j$ be vertices. Then $j$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of $i$ in the graph obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$.

results.title: Deleting an edge removes the out-neighbor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, given by its adjacency matrix, and let $i$ and $j$ be vertices. After the edge from $i$ to $j$ is deleted from $G$ (whether or not $G$ had that edge), $j$ is not an out-neighbor of $i$.

results.title: Out-neighbors after adding an edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j, b$ be vertices. Then $b$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of $i$ in the graph obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ if and only if $b = j$ or $b$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of $i$ in $m$.

results.title: Out-degree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The out-degree of a vertex $i$ of a directed graph given by an adjacency matrix is the number of its out-neighbors, that is, the number of vertices $j$ such that there is an edge from $i$ to $j$.

results.title: Vertices of the empty graph have out-degree zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n$, every vertex of the empty directed graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ has out-degree $0$.

results.title: Heath's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the dependency `R₁ ∩ R₂ → R₁` holds in a relation `r` over `R₁ ∪ R₂`, then `r` is the natural join of its projections onto `R₁` and `R₂`.

results.title: Satisfying a set of dependencies on a scheme
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A relation $r$ satisfies a finite set $F$ of functional dependencies on a set $S$ of attributes when every dependency $X \to Y$ with $X, Y \subseteq S$ that is derivable from $F$ by Armstrong's axioms holds in $r$.

results.title: Lossless binary decompositions from derivable dependencies
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies and let $R_1$, $R_2$ be sets of attributes. If $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_1$ or $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_2$ is derivable from $F$ by Armstrong's axioms, then for every value type $D$ the decomposition of $R_1 \cup R_2$ into $R_1$ and $R_2$ is lossless for $F$ with values in $D$.

results.title: Converse of the lossless-join test for two schemes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies, let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be schemes whose union is the set of all attributes, and let $D$ be a value type containing at least two distinct elements. If the decomposition of $R_1 \cup R_2$ into $R_1$ and $R_2$ is lossless for $F$ with values in $D$, then $F$ derives $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_1$ or $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_2$.

results.title: Lossless binary decompositions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies, let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be sets of attributes whose union is the set of all attributes, and suppose that the value type $D$ has two distinct elements. Then the decomposition into $R_1$ and $R_2$ is lossless for $F$ with values in $D$ if and only if $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_1$ or $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_2$ is derivable from $F$ by Armstrong's axioms.

results.title: Unit relation of the natural join
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The relation containing only the empty tuple, the unit of the natural join.

results.title: Join of the projections of a relation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a relation $r$ (a finite set of tuples) and a list of schemes $S_1, \dots, S_n$, this is the natural join of the projections $\pi_{S_1} r, \dots, \pi_{S_n} r$, computed as $\pi_{S_1} r \bowtie (\pi_{S_2} r \bowtie (\cdots \bowtie (\pi_{S_n} r \bowtie U)))$, where $U$ is the relation containing only the empty tuple; for the empty list it is $U$.

results.title: Union of a list of schemes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $S_1, \dots, S_n$ of schemes (finite sets of attributes), this is the union $S_1 \cup \dots \cup S_n$; for the empty list it is the empty set.

results.title: Membership in a join of projections
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $r$ be a relation over a schema $R$ and let $S_1, \dots, S_n$ be a list of schemes, each contained in $R$. A tuple $t$ belongs to the natural join of the projections $\pi_{S_1} r, \dots, \pi_{S_n} r$ if and only if $t$ is a tuple over $S_1 \cup \dots \cup S_n$ and, for every $i$, the restriction of $t$ to $S_i$ belongs to $\pi_{S_i} r$.

results.title: Boyce–Codd normal form
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A scheme $S$ is in Boyce–Codd normal form for a set $F$ of functional dependencies when, for every dependency $X \to Y$ derivable from $F$ with $X, Y \subseteq S$, either $Y \subseteq X$ or $F$ derives $X \to S$ (that is, $X$ is a superkey of $S$).

results.title: BCNF violations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies and $S$ a scheme, and write $X^+$ for the attribute closure of a set $X$ of attributes under $F$. A set $X \subseteq S$ violates BCNF in $S$ when $S \not\subseteq X^+$ and $X^+ \cap S \not\subseteq X$, that is, when the closure $X^+ \cap S$ of $X$ within $S$ is neither $X$ nor $S$.

results.title: Candidate BCNF violations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $l$ of attributes and a set $S$ of attributes, the candidate violations of BCNF in $S$ are all subsets of the set of attributes that occur in $l$ and lie in $S$, listed once each. Duplicates in $l$ are removed first, so there are $2^k$ candidates when $k$ distinct attributes of $l$ lie in $S$.

results.title: BCNF decomposition with bounded depth
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies, $l$ a list of attributes, $n$ a natural number and $S$ a scheme. For $n = 0$ the result is the list $[S]$. For $n > 0$, the candidate violations of BCNF in $S$ built from $l$ are searched in order for the first $X$ that violates BCNF in $S$ for $F$. If there is none, the result is $[S]$. Otherwise, with $X^+$ the attribute closure of $X$ under $F$, the result is the…

results.title: BCNF decomposition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies, $l$ a list of attributes and $S$ a scheme. The BCNF decomposition of $S$ for $F$ and $l$ is the BCNF decomposition with bounded depth run on $S$ with depth bound $|S|$. At each step, if some candidate violation of BCNF in the current scheme $T$ built from $l$ violates BCNF in $T$ for $F$, the first such $X$ is used: with $X^+$ the attribute closure of $X$ under $F$, $T$…

results.title: The BCNF decomposition is lossless
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies, $l$ a list of attributes and $S$ a set of attributes, and let $r$ be a relation over $S$ that satisfies every dependency $X \to Y$ derivable from $F$ with $X, Y \subseteq S$. Then $r$ is the natural join of its projections onto the schemes of the BCNF decomposition of $S$ for $F$ and $l$.

results.title: The BCNF decomposition produces BCNF schemes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies and $l$ a list containing every attribute. Then for every scheme $S$, every scheme in the BCNF decomposition of $S$ for $F$ and $l$ is in Boyce–Codd normal form for $F$.

results.title: Equivalent sets of functional dependencies
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two sets $F$ and $G$ of functional dependencies are equivalent when $F$ derives every dependency of $G$ and $G$ derives every dependency of $F$.

results.title: Projection of the dependency closure onto a scheme
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite set $F$ of functional dependencies and a set $S$ of attributes, this is the finite set of all dependencies $X \to Y$ with $X, Y \subseteq S$ that are derivable from $F$ by Armstrong's axioms, that is, the projection onto $S$ of the closure $F^+$ of $F$.

results.title: Dependency-preserving decompositions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A list $l$ of schemes is dependency-preserving for a set $F$ of functional dependencies when every dependency of $F$ is derivable from the union, over the schemes $S$ of $l$, of the sets of dependencies $X \to Y$ derivable from $F$ with $X, Y \subseteq S$.

results.title: Synthesis
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $G$ of functional dependencies and a set of attributes $K$, the synthesized decomposition is the list of schemes consisting of $K$ followed by, for each dependency $X \to Y$ of $G$ in order, the scheme $X \cup Y$.

results.title: Synthesis is dependency-preserving
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies and $G$ a list of functional dependencies equivalent to $F$ (each derives every dependency of the other). Then for every set of attributes $K$, the decomposition synthesized from $G$ and $K$, with one scheme $X \cup Y$ for each dependency $X \to Y$ of $G$ together with the scheme $K$, is dependency-preserving for $F$.

results.title: Synthesis is lossless
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a cover `G` of `F` and a superkey `K` of all attributes, every relation over all attributes satisfying `F` is the join of its projections onto the synthesized schemes.

results.title: Claims and allocations of processes
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A system with processes $P$ and resource types $R$ consists of two maps $\mathrm{claim}, \mathrm{alloc} : P \to (R \to \mathbb{N})$, where $\mathrm{claim}(p)$ is the maximum demand of process $p$ for each resource type and $\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ is the amount of each resource type currently allocated to $p$. No inequality between the two is required.

results.title: Remaining need
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The remaining need of a process $p$ in a system $S$ is the resource vector $\mathrm{claim}(p) - \mathrm{alloc}(p)$: the maximum claim of $p$ minus its current allocation, computed for each resource type by truncated subtraction of natural numbers, so it is $0$ for every resource type where the allocation exceeds the claim.

results.title: Safe sequence

results.summary: Let $S$ be a system with processes $P$ and resource types $R$, where process $p$ has maximum claim $\mathrm{claim}(p)$ and allocation $\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ in $R \to \mathbb{N}$. A list $p_1, \dots, p_k$ of processes is a safe sequence from the free resource vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ when, for each $i$, the remaining need $\mathrm{claim}(p_i) - \mathrm{alloc}(p_i)$ (truncated at zero) is at most…

results.title: Safe state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $S$ be a system of claims and allocations with processes $P$ and resource types $R$. A list of pending processes is safe from the free resource vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ when it has no repetitions and some permutation of it is a safe sequence from $w$: the pending processes can all finish, one after another, in some order.

results.title: Safe sequences are monotone in the free resources
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a system of processes with maximum claims and current allocations, and let $\sigma$ be a list of processes. If $\sigma$ is a safe sequence for $S$ from a vector $w$ of free resources (a natural number for each resource type), and $w \le w'$ componentwise, then $\sigma$ is also a safe sequence for $S$ from $w'$.

results.title: Removing a process from a safe sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a system of processes with maximum claims and current allocations, let $w$ be a vector of free resources (a natural number for each resource type), and let $\sigma$ be a list of processes that is a safe sequence for $S$ from $w$. If $p$ occurs in $\sigma$, then the list obtained from $\sigma$ by deleting the first occurrence of $p$ is a safe sequence for $S$ from $w + \mathrm{alloc}(p)$, where…

results.title: A safe state is not deadlocked
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a system of processes with maximum claims and current allocations, let $w$ be a vector of free resources (a natural number for each resource type), and let $L$ be a nonempty list of pending processes. If $S$ is safe from $w$ for $L$, then some process $p$ in $L$ has remaining need $\mathrm{need}(p) \le w$ componentwise, so it can be given its whole remaining need.

results.summary: Let $S$ be a system with processes $P$ and a finite set $R$ of resource types, where process $p$ has maximum claim $\mathrm{claim}(p)$ and allocation $\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ in $R \to \mathbb{N}$. Given a fuel $n \in \mathbb{N}$, a free resource vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ and a list of pending processes, the algorithm succeeds if the list is empty. results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $S$ be a system of claims and allocations with processes $P$ and a finite set $R$ of resource types. Given a free resource vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ and a list of pending processes, the algorithm fails if the list has a repetition. results.title: Correctness of the safety algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every system $S$ of claims and allocations over a finite set $R$ of resource types, every free resource vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ and every list of pending processes, the banker's safety algorithm succeeds on $w$ and the list if and only if the list is a safe state from $w$.

results.title: Remaining need after a grant
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Granted requests lead to safe states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a system of processes with maximum claims and current allocations, $a$ the vector of free resources, $L$ the list of pending processes, $p$ a process and $r$ a resource vector. If the resource-request algorithm grants the request of $r$ by $p$, returning the free vector $a'$ and the system $S'$, then $S'$ is safe from $a'$ for $L$.

part.title: Lamport clocks
api: Happened-before goes forward in the execution

results.title: Event
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: An event of an execution, for a type $P$ of processes, consists of the process in $P$ it belongs to and, if it is a receipt, a natural number: the position in the execution of the event whose message it receives. The structure does not require that position to be earlier than the event itself.

results.title: Well-formed executions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An execution $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ is well formed when every receipt names an earlier event: whenever $e_j$ receives the message sent by the event at position $i$, then $i < j$.

results.title: One step of happened-before
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In an execution, position $i$ precedes position $j$ by one step when $i < j$, both positions hold events, and either the two events belong to the same process or the event at $j$ receives the message of the event at $i$.

results.title: Happened-before
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Lamport's happened-before relation on the positions of an execution is the transitive closure of one step of happened-before: $a$ happened before $b$ when there is a chain $a = i_0, i_1, \dots, i_k = b$ with $k \ge 1$ in which each $i_m$ precedes $i_{m+1}$ by one step.

results.title: Happened-before goes forward in the execution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If position $a$ happened before position $b$ in an execution, then $a < b$.

results.title: One step of the Lamport clock algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The state is a counter $c(p) \in \mathbb{N}$ for each process $p$ together with the timestamps assigned so far. An event $e$ of process $p$ gets the timestamp $t = \max(c(p), s) + 1$, where $s$ is the timestamp already assigned at the position that $e$ receives from; $s = 0$ if $e$ is not a receipt or if no timestamp has been assigned at that position. The step sets $c(p)$ to $t$ and appends $t$ to the timestamps.

results.title: Running the Lamport clock algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The clock algorithm over an execution applies one step of the algorithm to each event in order, starting from all process counters $0$ and no timestamps. The result is the final counters together with the timestamps assigned to the events, in order.

results.title: Lamport timestamps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Lamport timestamps $t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}$ of an execution $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ are computed by Lamport's clock algorithm. Every process keeps a counter, initially $0$. For $k = 0, \dots, n-1$ in turn, let $c$ be the current counter of the process of $e_k$, and let $m = t_i$ if $e_k$ receives the message sent by the event at position $i$ with $i < k$, and $m = 0$ otherwise. Then $t_k = \max(c, m) + 1$, and the…

results.title: Appending events does not change earlier timestamps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be an execution, and extend it by appending further events. For every $i < n$, the Lamport timestamp of the event at position $i$ is the same in the extended execution as in the original one.

results.title: Process counters dominate their timestamps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: After the Lamport clock algorithm has run over an execution, the counter of each process is at least the timestamp of every event of that process in the execution.

results.title: A timestamp depends only on a prefix containing its event
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be an execution and let $i < k \le n$. The Lamport timestamp of $e_i$ in the whole execution equals its Lamport timestamp in the prefix $e_0, \dots, e_{k-1}$.

results.title: One step of happened-before raises the timestamp
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If position $i$ precedes position $j$ by one step of happened-before in an execution, then the Lamport timestamp of $i$ is smaller than the Lamport timestamp of $j$.

results.title: A receipt is stamped later than its send
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be a well-formed execution and let $t_k$ be the Lamport timestamp of $e_k$. If $j < n$ and $e_j$ receives the message sent by the event at position $i$, then $t_i < t_j$.

results.title: Lamport timestamps increase along each process
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be an execution and let $t_k$ be the Lamport timestamp of $e_k$. If $i < j < n$ and $e_i$ and $e_j$ belong to the same process, then $t_i < t_j$.

results.title: The clock condition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In every execution, if the event at position $a$ happened before the event at position $b$, then the Lamport timestamp of $a$ is smaller than the Lamport timestamp of $b$ (Lamport 1978).

results.title: Happened-before relates positions of the execution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If position $a$ happened before position $b$ in an execution, then the execution has an event at position $a$ and an event at position $b$.

results.title: Lamport's total order
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Fix a linear order on the processes. In an execution $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ with Lamport timestamps $t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}$, position $a$ precedes position $b$ when $a < n$, $b < n$, and either $t_a < t_b$, or $t_a = t_b$ and the process of $e_a$ is smaller than the process of $e_b$.

results.title: Lamport's total order extends happened-before
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In every execution, if the event at position $a$ happened before the event at position $b$, then position $a$ precedes position $b$ in Lamport's total order.

results.title: Lamport's order is total
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In every execution, for any two distinct positions $a \ne b$ that both hold events, $a$ precedes $b$ or $b$ precedes $a$ in Lamport's total order.
